ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Consider the following simple model of a bow and arrow. An ideal elastic string has a spring constant $k=10 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}$ and relaxed length $L=1 \mathrm{~m}$ which is attached to the ends of an inflexible fixed steel rod of the same length $L$ as shown below. A small ball of mass $m=2 \mathrm{~kg}$ and the thread are pulled by its midpoint away from the rod until each individual part of the thread have the same length of the rod, as shown below. What is the speed of the ball in meters per seconds right after it stops accelerating? Assume the whole setup is carried out in zero gravity.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure is a fixed vertical steel rod, labeled with length L. The two ends of the elastic string are fixed respectively to the upper and lower ends of the steel rod; the midpoint of the string is pulled out to the right and connected to a small ball labeled with mass m, forming a symmetric triangle. In the figure, the two segments from the upper end of the steel rod to the small ball and from the lower end of the steel rod to the small ball are both labeled L. Reasoning: The problem gives the total relaxed length of the elastic string as L=1 m, the spring constant k=10 N/m, and the small ball mass m=2 kg. When pulled open, the two segments of string each have length L, so the total length of the elastic string is 2L. Relative to the relaxed total length L, the initial extension is 2L-L=L=1 m. Treat the whole elastic string as one spring; the initial elastic potential energy is (1/2)kL^2. The small ball accelerates in zero gravity until the elastic string returns to the relaxed total length L and the tension is zero; after that it no longer accelerates and moves uniformly. By conservation of mechanical energy, (1/2)kL^2=(1/2)mv^2, so v=L sqrt(k/m)=1*sqrt(10/2)=sqrt(5)=2.236... m/s, about 2.23 m/s.

method.method_draft: Compute the work done by the spring force along the ball’s symmetric path. From the image, model the ball as moving along the perpendicular bisector of the fixed rod; the rod endpoints are separated by L and each string half has length s. In the drawn initial state s=L, so the horizontal displacement from the rod midpoint is x0=sqrt(L^2-(L/2)^2)=sqrt(3)L/2. At the no-acceleration point the total string length is relaxed, so 2s=L and s=L/2, which corresponds to x=0. From the text use k=10 N/m, L=1 m, m=2 kg. For a uniform string with total spring constant k and relaxed length L, each half has stiffness 2k and relaxed length L/2, so the tension in each half is T=2k(s-L/2)=k(2s-L). The horizontal restoring force on the ball is F=2T(x/s). With s=sqrt(x^2+(L/2)^2), integrate the work from x0 to 0: W=integral 2k(2s-L)(x/s) dx = kL^2/2. Set W=(1/2)mv^2 to obtain v=sqrt(kL^2/m)=sqrt(5)=2.23 m/s.

An ideal elastic string has a spring constant $k=10 \, \mathrm{N}/\mathrm{m}$ and relaxed length $L=1 \, \mathrm{m}$ which is attached to the ends of an inflexible fixed steel rod of the same length $L$ as shown below. A small ball of mass $m=2 \, \mathrm{kg}$ and the thread are pulled by its midpoint away from the rod until each individual part of the thread has the same length as the rod, as shown below. What is the speed of the ball in meters per second right after it stops accelerating? Assume the whole setup is carried out in zero gravity.
ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
Image description: On the left side of the figure is a fixed vertical steel rod, labeled with length L. The two ends of the elastic string are fixed respectively to the upper and lower ends of the steel rod; the midpoint of the string is pulled out to the right and connected to a small ball labeled with mass m, forming a symmetric triangle. In the figure, the two segments from the upper end of the steel rod to the small ball and from the lower end of the steel rod to the small ball are both labeled L.

Reasoning: The problem gives the total relaxed length of the elastic string as L=1 m, the spring constant k=10 N/m, and the small ball mass m=2 kg. When pulled open, the two segments of string each have length L, so the total length of the elastic string is 2L. Relative to the relaxed total length L, the initial extension is 2L-L=L=1 m. Treat the whole elastic string as one spring; the initial elastic potential energy is (1/2)kL^2. The small ball accelerates in zero gravity until the elastic string returns to the relaxed total length L and the tension is zero; after that it no longer accelerates and moves uniformly. By conservation of mechanical energy, (1/2)kL^2=(1/2)mv^2, so v=L sqrt(k/m)=1*sqrt(10/2)=sqrt(5)=2.236... m/s, about 2.23 m/s.
